precepts.text: The counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God. That is how speaking with Ahithophel was regarded: like the word of God came from heaven. That is the sense of receiving a man as an angel; it is not Michael and Uriel coming down from the heavens to talk to you.
precepts.point: How do you go about not being beguiled? If you study, you do not willingly give yourself over to men that will deceive you by handling the word of God deceitfully. Study to shew thyself approved, that you will be able to withstand these men.

note.label: Deceived by Enticing Words: Colossians 2

precepts.why:
“And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.”

That is how speaking with Ahithophel was regarded: as if you enquired at an angel of God, like the word of God came from heaven. Ahithophel was a man, but his counsel was received like an oracle, both by David and by Absalom.

That is the sense of the worshipping of angels in Colossians 2:18. You thought Michael and Uriel came from the heavens to talk to you? That is not what it means. It is the worshipping of men that speak so well, with enticing words, with the wisdom of this world. Paul spoke of “the wisdom of this world” and “the princes of this world, that come to nought”. It goes into the same thing.

So “a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels” is you voluntarily humbling yourself in the worshipping of man: receiving a man's word as if it were an oracle of God, the way they did with Ahithophel. Let no man beguile you of your reward that way.

precepts.text: The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God, so was all his counsel with both David and Absalom.
precepts.point: Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was said to be like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David prayed the Most High would turn that counsel into foolishness, and sent his friend Hushai to act like Absalom's servant so he could listen to Ahithophel's counsel and intervene. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

precepts.why:
“And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.”

That is why it mattered when “one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David, weeping as he went up mount Olivet, prayed, “O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

And he did not stop at praying. He sent his friend Hushai the Archite back to the city to say unto Absalom, “I will be thy servant, O king”, so he could hear Ahithophel’s counsel and intervene: “then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.” Everything he heard would go to Zadok and Abiathar the priests and on to David by their two sons. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

precepts.text: The Most High would raise up evil out of David's own house and give his wives to his neighbour in the sight of the sun, done before all Israel because David did it secretly.
precepts.point: Ahithophel counselled Absalom to lie with the ten concubines David left, in the sight of all Israel, on the roof of the house. This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12, that David's wives would be taken and one would lie with them in the sight of the sun, and that what David did secretly would be done before all Israel. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. The Most High keeps mercy and forgives, but by no means clears the guilty, so even when we come in and repent, we still must remember the fear of the Most High, for there is but one step between us and death.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

precepts.why:
The Most High told David by Nathan, “Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun. For thou didst it secretly: but I will do this thing before all Israel, and before the sun.”

Here it is. Ahithophel counselled Absalom, “Go in unto thy father’s concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father”. So “they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.” The ten concubines David left, on the roof of the house, in the sight of the sun.

This is the exact fulfillment of what the Most High spoke in chapter 12. It was not coincidence or irony; it was prophesied to happen. What David did secretly was done before all Israel, by evil raised up out of his own house, and none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

precepts.why:
“For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.”

What came on David from Absalom and Ahithophel came for his own faults, as the Most High spoke in chapter 12; none of it would have happened if David had not done what he did. There is no glory in being buffeted for your faults. The suffering that is acceptable with God is to do well, suffer for it, and take it patiently.

precepts.text: Ahithophel's counsel to defile David's concubines, and how his counsel was esteemed as the oracle of God with both David and Absalom.
precepts.point: Now he asks Absalom to let him choose out twelve thousand men to pursue David that same night while David was weary and weak handed, to smite the king only and bring back all the people. He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the one who killed King David.

note.label: 2 Samuel 17: The Counsel of the Lord Shall Stand

precepts.why:
Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give counsel among you what we shall do.” Ahithophel answered, “Go in unto thy father’s concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.” That was already wicked counsel, before he ever asked for twelve thousand men.

Ahithophel was David’s own counselor turned traitor, being the devil the Bible speaks of, working deceit and betrayal from inside the gates of Israel. And “the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.” That tells you he was very influential and had the gift of gab, so persuasive that his advice sounded almost biblical.

So when he said, “Let me now choose out twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night”, to come upon him “while he is weary and weak handed” and “smite the king only”, Absalom was hearing it from the man everyone listened to. He wanted the victory and the bragging rights of being the one who killed King David.

precepts.text: Shimei came out cursing David, casting stones, and calling him a bloody man and a man of Belial as he fled Jerusalem.
precepts.point: Abishai and the sons of Zeruiah said Shimei should be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed, but David rebuked them as adversaries, asking whether any man should be put to death that day in Israel when he knew he was king. He swore Shimei would not die. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

note.label: 2 Samuel 19: The King Returns to His House

precepts.why:
When king David came to Bahurim, Shimei the son of Gera, of the family of the house of Saul, “came forth, and cursed still as he came. And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.” He cried, “Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial”.

That was David in a low state, fleeing Jerusalem, surrounded by his mighty men, and Shimei cursed him to his face. Now the king was coming back, and the same Shimei hasted down with a thousand men of Benjamin and fell down before him at Jordan: “Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me, neither do thou remember that which thy servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem”. He confessed, “For thy servant doth know that I have sinned”.

Abishai said, “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” But David rebuked the sons of Zeruiah as adversaries: “shall there any man be put to death this day in Israel? for do not I know that I am this day king over Israel?” He said to Shimei, “Thou shalt not die”, and swore it. David understood grace long before the New Testament, for grace has always been around.

precepts.text: When Absalom sought the kingdom, David let Shimei curse him, saying the Lord had bidden him to curse, and "it may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day." The Lord is the one who allowed the cursing, and through the affliction received from man, David would be repaid good. Being cursed and afflicted, we receive a reward for overcoming it.
precepts.point: Punishment for sins drives you back to the Most High. This is Hosea 5:15; when affliction comes we go back to the Lord, and that is how the Lord gets us back. Even people in the world call on the Lord when things go wrong, though he does not always hear them.

note.label: Psalm 42: Panting After God in the Midst of Affliction

precepts.why:
David's enemies reproached him daily, and he had lived it before. When Absalom sought the kingdom and Shimei cursed him, David said, “so let him curse, because the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David.” “Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it? let him alone, and let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him. It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day.”

The Lord is the one who allowed the cursing, and through the affliction received from man, David would be repaid good. That is how to hear “Where is thy God?” from the mouths of the enemy: being cursed and afflicted, we receive a reward for overcoming it. So the soul is not to be cast down but to hope in God, “for I shall yet praise him”.

points: And when king David came to Bahurim, behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera: he came forth, and cursed still as he came.

So David saw this as an opportunity to turn back to the Lord, repenting for what he did to Uriah. But what I want you to see is, whether it be lust and covetousness, then came about the hatred to the point where you wanted to put that brother to death, and did. The same exact way envy, jealousy, rebellion against God caused King Saul to do it to King David. So everyone has their path, but that icing on the cake is bitterness for everyone.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: The Lord hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose stead thou hast reigned; and the Lord hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son. So here it is. This brother from the house of Saul, meaning from the tribe of Benjamin, is now showing his hatred or disdain for King David for the kingdom being translated over to him. He is blaming King David for Saul's death. He is blaming King David for everything. And in that anger he begins to cast stones at David and his mighty men. Now he is saying, the fact that Absalom is hunting for you, you deserve it, because of all the bloodiness that you did. Now Absalom is doing it to you.
And, behold, thou art taken in thy mischief, because thou art a bloody man.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: Then said Abishai the son of Zeruiah unto the king, Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: And the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? so let him curse, because the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? So King David said, you know what, let this man curse me out. Now David is a king. His mighty men are ready to put this dude to death. But he says, let him be. He said it had to be the Lord that spoke unto him and told him to come and curse me.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: What I want everyone to see is how the spirit of bitterness will go from person to person, and all of the situations that caused it are varying, or have variations of how it was built upon for each person. For instance, for some the first thing that might be rolling in is envy. It might start with envy, then it leads to hatred and bitterness later on. For others it may be covetousness, like we just saw with King David. For others it might be disobedience. But it has a beginning point and there are building blocks upon that.

And David said to Abishai, and to all his servants, Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now may this Benjamite do it? let him alone, and let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him. Now King David is in his repentant state. He said, let him curse, because the Lord sent him to curse me.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: It may be that the Lord will look on mine affliction, and that the Lord will requite me good for his cursing this day. And my hope is that in this man cursing me for the evil I did, I pray he will have mercy. This is why David is a man after the Lord's heart, because he was able to acknowledge his errors. He is able to acknowledge his faults, his shortcomings, his sins, and always go to the Lord asking for mercy.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: And as David and his men went by the way, Shimei went along on the hill's side over against him, and cursed as he went, and threw stones at him, and cast dust. So as they are walking, this man went up on the hillside above them, following them, throwing stones at them.

note.label: The Building Blocks of Bitterness

points: When David was past the top of the hill, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with saddled asses, two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred bunches of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. When David asked where his master's son was, Ziba said Mephibosheth abode in Jerusalem, saying the house of Israel would restore him the kingdom of his father. So David gave Ziba all that pertained to Mephibosheth.

Ziba came with gifts, and when David asked about Mephibosheth, Ziba claimed Mephibosheth thought the kingdom was about to be restored to him, which was not true. On that word David handed Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

points: Shimei was of the house of Saul, and Saul was the wicked one who tried to kill David; it was by the hand of the Most High that Saul did not succeed. Yet Shimei cursed David as if David were in the wrong, because word gets around, people gossip and blame, and he saw David at a low state and went to rub it in his face. That is the mindset of some people in Israel as well.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

points: Abishai the son of Zeruiah asked why this dead dog should curse the king, and offered to go take off his head. But the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Most High hath said unto him, Curse David; who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?

David rolled with mighty men of war, so Abishai was ready to take Shimei's head off his shoulders. But David said to let him curse, for if it was of the Most High, then let him do it. Just as the Most High brings people to our forums and classrooms who bicker and try to bring confusion, it is of the Most High, sometimes to test the patience of those who pray for patience.

note.label: 2 Samuel 16: Ziba, Shimei's Cursing, and Absalom Defiles the Concubines

David reasoned that if his own son sought his life, this Benjamite was nothing; the Most High was doing this, so let him curse. It may be the Most High will look on all that was done to David and bless him in front of them, the same as when people try to bring us down and the Most High blesses us before them, which is why this congregation has grown exponentially.
